name: RabbitMQ
description: Protects against destructive RabbitMQ operations like deleting queues/exchanges, \ purging queues, deleting vhosts, and resetting cluster state.

destructive_patterns.name: rabbitmqadmin-delete-queue
destructive_patterns.description: rabbitmqadmin delete queue permanently deletes a queue.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a queue permanently removes all messages and bindings. \ Consumers will disconnect, and producers will fail unless they handle \ the missing queue. Undelivered messages are lost.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - rabbitmqadmin list queues: Review queues first \ - rabbitmqadmin purge queue: Remove messages but keep the queue \ - Set TTL or max-length policies for automatic cleanup

destructive_patterns.name: rabbitmqadmin-delete-exchange
destructive_patterns.description: rabbitmqadmin delete exchange removes an exchange and its bindings.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting an exchange removes all bindings to queues. Messages published \ to this exchange will be lost unless an alternate exchange is configured. \ Publishers may not receive errors if they don't use confirms.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - rabbitmqadmin list exchanges: Review exchanges first \ - rabbitmqadmin list bindings: Check dependent bindings \ - Rebind queues to a new exchange before deletion

destructive_patterns.name: rabbitmqadmin-purge-queue
destructive_patterns.description: rabbitmqadmin purge queue deletes ALL messages in the queue.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Purging a queue deletes all messages immediately. Messages that were \ waiting to be consumed are permanently lost. This cannot be undone.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - rabbitmqadmin show queue: Check message count first \ - Consume and process messages instead of purging \ - Set message TTL for automatic expiration

destructive_patterns.name: rabbitmqctl-delete-vhost
destructive_patterns.description: rabbitmqctl delete_vhost removes a vhost and all its resources.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Deleting a vhost removes ALL queues, exchanges, bindings, policies, \ and user permissions within that vhost. This is a complete wipe of \ that namespace.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - rabbitmqctl list_vhosts: Review vhosts first \ - rabbitmqctl list_queues -p <vhost>: Check resources in vhost \ - Export definitions before deletion

destructive_patterns.name: rabbitmqctl-forget-cluster-node
destructive_patterns.description: rabbitmqctl forget_cluster_node permanently removes a node from the cluster.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Forgetting a cluster node removes it from the cluster metadata. Use this \ only for permanently failed nodes. Mirrored queues may lose replicas, \ and quorum queues may lose availability if quorum is affected.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - rabbitmqctl cluster_status: Review cluster state first \ - Try to recover the node instead of forgetting \ - Ensure quorum is maintained after removal

destructive_patterns.name: rabbitmqctl-reset
destructive_patterns.description: rabbitmqctl reset wipes all configuration, queues, and bindings on the node.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Reset returns the node to a blank state, removing all exchanges, queues, \ bindings, users, vhosts, and permissions. The node is removed from any \ cluster it was part of.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Export definitions before reset \ - Use stop_app/start_app for service restart without data loss \ - Consider forget_cluster_node for cluster membership changes only

destructive_patterns.name: rabbitmqctl-force-reset
destructive_patterns.description: rabbitmqctl force_reset wipes node data and can break cluster state.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
Force reset ignores cluster state and wipes the node unconditionally. \ This can leave the cluster in an inconsistent state where other nodes \ still expect this node to exist.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Try rabbitmqctl reset first (safer) \ - Coordinate with cluster members before force reset \ - Document the cluster state for recovery
